title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Hickmott LM, Chilibeck PD, Shaw KA, Butcher SJ
population: Resistance-trained individuals; 15 studies, 6 on load autoregulation (repetitions-in-reserve rated exertion or velocity-based training against percentage-based prescription) and 9 on volume autoregulation (velocity-loss thresholds). Not runners.
findings: Searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and SPORTDiscus under PRISMA; the protocol was registered (PROSPERO CRD42021240506).

Autoregulated load prescription (repetitions-in-reserve based rating of perceived exertion, or velocity-based training) and standardised percentage-based prescription did not differ for 1RM strength (MD 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46, p = 0.09, SMD 0.21).

With sets and relative intensity equated, velocity-loss thresholds of 25% or less gave greater 1RM strength than thresholds above 25% (MD 2.32 kg, 95% CI 0.33-4.31, p = 0.02, SMD 0.23) and less hypertrophy (MD 0.61 cm2, p = 0.03).
The authors conclude that autoregulated and standardised load prescription produced similar improvements in strength.
limitations: The abstract gives the number of studies, not the number of participants; resistance-trained lifters, not runners or novices; the comparison is of prescription methods over short interventions on 1RM and muscle size, with no running, economy or injury outcome. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: The only synthesis in the corpus that compares ways of choosing the load: an effort-based (repetitions-in-reserve) prescription and a percentage-of-maximum prescription gave similar strength gains in trained lifters. It supports an effort target as no worse than a percentage, not as better, and says nothing about double progression or about runners.
No evidence here on the novice or recreational lifter, who is the usual user of the strength page; the load-progression rule stays a default (grade D).
